item.title: Oma Bluefin Tuna: Japan's Prized Catch — Aomori Guide
item.description: Oma bluefin tuna, line-caught off Cape Oma at the very northern tip of Honshu, is among the most prized fish in Japan — a single Oma tuna once sold for record millions at Tokyo’s market. At the port, you can eat this melt-in-the-mouth ‘black diamond’ as sashimi and sushi, straight from the source. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Oma, Shimokita, Aomori Hours Restaurant hours (some seasonal) Admission Varies; premium tuna sets Time needed About 1 hour Best time Autumn–winter (peak tuna season) What to Try Melt-in-the-mouth Oma bluefin sashimi and sushi.

item.title: Hokkaido Seafood Guide: Crab, Uni, Kaisendon & Where to Eat
item.description: Cold, rich northern seas make Hokkaido a paradise for seafood — arguably the best in Japan. This is the place to feast on sweet king and snow crab, melt-in-the-mouth sea urchin (uni), glistening salmon roe (ikura), plump scallops and the freshest sashimi. The signature way to enjoy it all is a kaisendon — a bowl of rice heaped with a rainbow of raw seafood — devoured at a bustling morning market.

item.title: Kyoto Cooking Class Guide: Learn Japanese Home Cooking
item.description: A cooking class is one of the most rewarding things a food-loving visitor can do in Kyoto — and one of the few souvenirs you can take home and use forever. In a few hours, a friendly local instructor teaches you to make real Japanese home cooking — washoku staples, Kyoto’s vegetable-forward obanzai, sushi, ramen, or delicate wagashi sweets — often after a guided shop through Nishiki Market to choose your ingredients.

item.title: Otaru Guide: Canal, Glassworks & Day Trip from Sapporo
item.description: A short train ride from Sapporo, Otaru is a postcard-pretty port town built on a once-booming herring and trade economy. Its centrepiece is the Otaru Canal, lined with handsome stone warehouses and Victorian-style gas lamps — impossibly romantic at dusk and magical under winter snow. The old merchant streets now brim with glassblowing studios, music-box shops, sushi counters and sake breweries. Easy to reach and full of charm, Otaru is one of Hokkaido’s most popular day trips.

item.title: Tokyo Sushi Making Class Guide: Learn from a Trained Itamae
item.description: Sushi looks deceptively simple — a slice of fish on a mound of rice — but every element conceals years of craft. In a Tokyo sushi-making class, a trained itamae (sushi chef) reveals those secrets: how to season and handle the rice, how to wield a Japanese knife, and how to shape nigiri and roll maki with the right pressure and form. You leave not only having eaten beautiful sushi you made yourself, but with knife and rice fundamentals that quietly change how you eat — and make — sushi for the rest of your life.

item.title: Tsukiji Outer Market Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Food Morning
item.description: For 83 years, Tsukiji was the largest fish market on Earth — the beating heart of Tokyo’s relationship with seafood, where billions of yen of tuna changed hands before dawn. In 2018 the famous wholesale auctions moved to a modern facility in Toyosu, but here’s what most visitors don’t realise: the part you actually want to visit never left. The bustling Outer Market (Tsukiji Jogai Shijo) — the warren of stalls, knife shops, and tiny restaurants where the public eats — is still right where it always was, still serving some of the freshest, most exciting food in Tokyo, every morning.

item.title: Best Restaurants in Kanagawa: Yokohama, Kamakura & Beyond
item.description: Kanagawa’s food scene is one of the most distinctive in Japan, shaped by the prefecture’s dual identity as an ancient capital and a 19th-century international port. This is the birthplace of Japan’s most copied ramen style, the home of the country’s largest Chinatown, and the region where the Japanese Navy invented curry as we know it. Eating your way through Kanagawa is a journey through modern Japanese food history. Ie-kei Ramen (家系ラーメン) — Yokohama’s Gift to Japan No single city has had more influence on Japanese ramen culture than Yokohama.

item.title: Best Restaurants in Tokyo: Lunch & Dinner
item.description: Tokyo has more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city on earth — including more starred sushi counters than the rest of the world combined. But the city’s real food culture runs far deeper than Michelin stars. This guide covers the best places to eat at every budget, from a ¥600 standing sushi bar to the counter where a master has been pressing rice for 40 years. 🍣 Sushi Standing Sushi Bars — The Tokyo Insider’s Lunch The best-value sushi experience in Tokyo isn’t an omakase counter — it’s a tachi-gui (standing) sushi bar in Tsukiji’s outer market or around major train stations.
